item.title: Bangladesh First: A Nation Cannot Rise Unless Justice Reaches Everyone. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
When we say “Bangladesh First,” we are making a promise that this country, our country, will place the wellbeing of ordinary citizens above every competing interest. It is an emotional phrase, and rightly so, because after more than fifty years of independence, the question of what truly comes first for the average Bangladeshi remains deeply important.
Ask a farmer waiting years for a land dispute to be resolved. Ask a small trader who has spent his savings fighting a case he never expected to face. Ask a mother whose son spent months in custody before the charge against him was found to lack sufficient basis. Their answer to “what comes first” may not be economic growth figures or infrastructure projects. Their answer may be one word: justice. Justice that arrives on time, treats people with dignity, and does not exhaust a person’s spirit in the process of proving their innocence.
This is the conversation this anniversary piece hopes to open. Not about politics. Not about any single institution, party, or individual. It is about something broader and urgent: the importance of strengthening public trust in our legal and justice processes, and what delay, unequal access, and weak accountability can cost the quiet, law-abiding majority.
The Silent Majority Pays the Price
There is a particular unfairness when ordinary people struggle to access timely justice. It rarely appears as one dramatic event. Instead, it can happen through delay, repeated paperwork, procedural complexity, limited access to quality legal support, and informal practices that may benefit those with greater resources or networks.
The people most affected are often not the wealthy or well-connected. They may have options, legal support, and the patience that comes with resources. The people most affected are usually ordinary citizens: shopkeepers, farmers, garment workers, students, retirees, and families who believe that if they have done nothing wrong, the system will eventually recognize that.
For many, justice may eventually come, but only after years of hearings, adjournments, and legal expenses that quietly weaken a family. A case that should take months may stretch into years. A hearing that should be routine may take much longer than expected. During that time, a business can collapse, children’s education can suffer, health can deteriorate from stress, and even when a person is cleared, social stigma may remain.
This is the invisible cost that slow and uneven legal processes place on the public. It is not only financial. It is also emotional, psychological, and social. A person who has been wrongly accused, delayed, or detained does not simply move on once the paperwork says they are free. The experience can leave behind anxiety, fear of authority, and a lasting doubt about whether truth alone is enough. When repeated across many families, this becomes more than a legal issue. It becomes a social trust issue, and even a public wellbeing issue.
Weak Accountability Is a Shared Challenge
It would be easy, but not helpful, to point fingers at one office, one department, or one group of people. The real picture is more complex. Weaknesses in a legal and judicial ecosystem are rarely created by one actor alone. They can grow wherever oversight is limited, accountability is inconsistent, and systems allow delay or discretion to affect people differently.
This can happen at many levels: when files move slowly, when citizens do not know how to navigate procedures, when evidence is not handled efficiently, when delay becomes a strategy, or when influence appears to matter more than merit. The powerful can often afford delay. The powerless often cannot.
None of this is unique to Bangladesh. Many countries, both developing and developed, continue to wrestle with delays, access gaps, and public trust challenges in their justice systems. What matters is not blaming any single group, but recognizing the pattern honestly enough to improve it.
The concern here is not any person or political side. The concern is a culture where shortcuts become normal, truth becomes negotiable, and ordinary citizens carry the cost of systemic weakness. If Bangladesh truly wants to come first, then integrity, fairness, and accountability must come first as well.
“Bangladesh First” Must Begin with Honesty First
There is a reason the words “Bangladesh First” resonate so strongly. They suggest a reordering of priorities, a decision to place the collective good above narrow interests, shortcuts, and convenient silence. But this cannot happen through slogans alone.
It requires an honest national commitment to a simple truth: a country cannot develop faster than its ability to deliver justice fairly. Roads, bridges, digital systems, and economic growth matter. But for a citizen caught in a long and uncertain legal process, development also means the confidence that truth will be heard, procedures will be fair, and dignity will be protected.
If we are serious about putting Bangladesh first, we must also put truth first, timeliness first, and equal treatment under law first, regardless of who is seeking justice and who is being asked to answer for their actions.
A nation that protects integrity in its justice processes protects not only courts and laws, but also the confidence of its people.
Building the Culture We Want, Starting from the Classroom
If integrity is not only a legal issue but also a cultural one, then the solution must also begin early. Laws can be amended, systems can be digitized, and courts can become more efficient. These steps are necessary. But they will not be enough if the next generation grows up believing that dishonesty and shortcuts are simply “how things are done.”
This is where education can play a larger role. Many students learn about the Constitution, fundamental rights, and government structures as exam-oriented facts. What is often missing is a practical understanding of civic ethics: what fairness means, why truth matters, how false accusations harm real people, why bribery weakens society, and why due process is not a burden but a protection for everyone.
This understanding cannot come from one textbook chapter alone. It should be woven into education through lessons on honesty, justice, empathy, and responsibility. Schools and universities can use debates on ethics, mock court activities, storytelling, drama, community service, and real-life case discussions to help students understand the human cost of injustice. When young people practice fairness rather than only memorize it, honesty becomes a habit, not an inconvenience.
Imagine a generation of Bangladeshis who grow up understanding that a lie told for short-term gain can damage another person’s life for years. That generation would not need integrity to be forced upon them. They would already see it as part of who they are.
A Happy, Safe Bangladesh Is the Goal Itself
At the heart of this conversation is a simple idea: people want to live without fear. Fear of being falsely implicated. Fear of losing years to a case that should have been resolved earlier. Fear of seeing an honest complaint delayed because the process feels too slow, too expensive, or too difficult to navigate.
A “happy Bangladesh” is not measured only by GDP charts or skyline photographs. It is also measured by whether an ordinary citizen can sleep peacefully knowing that if they are wronged, the system will treat them with dignity and seriousness.
A “safe Bangladesh” is not only about physical security. It is also about legal security: the confidence that truth matters, that due process works, and that no one’s future will be harmed simply because they lack power, money, or connections.
This is what “Bangladesh First” should mean: a country that chooses to strengthen justice before celebrating progress too loudly. A country that teaches its children early that honesty is strength, not weakness. A country that understands that every shortcut, every delay, and every failure of fairness quietly reduces public trust.
The ordinary people of this country, those who work, pay taxes, follow rules, wait patiently, and still try to believe in the system, deserve better than delay, fear, and uncertainty. They deserve a legal and justice system that heals rather than harms, protects rather than punishes the innocent, and moves with the urgency that justice requires.
If Bangladesh truly wants to come first, it must begin with a difficult but necessary commitment: to build not only more roads, buildings, and institutions, but also stronger habits of honesty, fairness, and trust. Only then can we say, without hesitation, that we have put our people, happy, safe, and justly treated, first.
The views expressed in this submission are personal and reflect a broader civic concern for institutional reform, not directed at any individual, group, or organization.

Equity must be at the heart of social support. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The BNP government’s family card program was rightfully seen as a positive, designed to ease the burden of rising living costs for low‑income households. For many families, it has indeed brought relief.
However, as per the report from Dhaka Tribune on the situation in Korail, residents say they have been left out despite being among Dhaka’s most vulnerable. This highlights a critical flaw: Support cannot be effective if it does not reach the right people.
This is a core challenge for social safety that Bangladesh must confront. Social protection schemes only work when they are equitable, transparent, and grounded in accurate data.
When deserving communities are excluded, when distribution lists are incomplete, or when selection processes rely on outdated or inconsistent criteria, the very purpose of these programs is undermined.
Korail is not an isolated case. Across the country, informal settlements, migrant workers, and low‑income households often fall through the cracks because they are not formally registered, lack documentation, or live in areas where administrative mapping is weak.
These are precisely the groups most in need of assistance, yet are frequently the ones left out.
We must do better. Whether that means updating beneficiary lists regularly, using digital tools to verify eligibility, or working closely with local administrations and community leaders who understand the realities on the ground, no stone must be left unturned.
Most important is ensuring that political influence or bureaucratic shortcuts do not distort who receives support.
Equity must be the guiding principle. Relief programs cannot be judged solely by how many cards are distributed, but by who receives them. If the poorest communities remain excluded, the program’s success is incomplete.
Social protection is not just about distribution. It is about fairness. And fairness demands that no vulnerable community is left behind.

item.title: From rice security to nutrition security: Bangladesh's next agricultural transformation. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A nation's history can sometimes be told through the story of a single bowl of rice. Bangladesh is one such nation. Half a century ago, the country's greatest challenge was ensuring enough food for its people. Food shortages, import dependence, and the painful memory of famine dominated national priorities. The central question was simple: Could Bangladesh produce enough food to feed its growing population? Today, the answer is a resounding yes.
Through scientific research, technological innovation, expanded irrigation, supportive public policies, and the dedication of millions of farmers, Bangladesh has transformed itself from a food-deficit nation into food surplus nation and one of the world's leading rice producers. Improved rice varieties developed by the Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI), together with better crop management, mechanization, and agricultural investment, have made rice security one of the country's greatest development achievements. Beyond eliminating hunger, it has strengthened economic growth and social stability.
Yet every success brings new responsibilities. Bangladesh's challenge today is no longer simply producing enough rice. It is ensuring that a growing population has access to nutritious, safe, and sustainable food despite climate change, shrinking farmland, and mounting pressure on natural resources.
Rice will remain the cornerstone of Bangladesh's food system for decades to come. However, future food policy must extend beyond calorie sufficiency to embrace nutrition security, food safety, environmental sustainability, and climate resilience. Bangladesh is therefore entering a new phase of agricultural development: The first national mission was to achieve rice security; the next is to build nutrition security upon that foundation.
This distinction is crucial. Food diversification is often misunderstood as moving away from rice. Bangladesh does not need to replace rice -- it needs to complement it. Rice is deeply rooted in the country's agroecology, farming systems, culture, and dietary habits, and it will continue to provide the largest share of dietary energy. Protecting rice production therefore remains essential.
At the same time, a healthy population requires more than calories. It needs adequate protein, healthy fats, vitamins, minerals, and dietary fibre. Rice provides the foundation of food security, while pulses, oilseeds, fruits, vegetables, livestock products, and other nutrient-rich foods complete the nutritional picture.
The future of Bangladesh's food policy, therefore, lies not in choosing between rice and diversification, but in building a rice-centered, nutrition-balanced food system that protects the achievements of the past while meeting the challenges of the future.
From rice security to nutrition security
This is not a shift away from rice. Rather, it represents the next stage in Bangladesh's agricultural development -- from ensuring rice security to achieving nutrition security. To examine how this transition might unfold, a long-term assessment of Bangladesh's food system was conducted for the period 2024–2074. The analysis projected future production and demand for seven major food groups -- rice, wheat, maize, potatoes, pulses, edible oils, and minor cereals -- and evaluated their contributions to national nutrition.
Rather than predicting a single future, the assessment explored two alternative development pathways. The first assumes that current trends in agricultural development continue, with gradual technological progress and existing policy priorities. This business-as-usual (BAU) scenario reflects the continuation of present investment patterns and historical productivity gains. The second, referred to as the balanced adjustment (BAdj) scenario, envisions a more deliberate transformation in which rice remains the cornerstone of national food security while greater policy emphasis is placed on nutritionally important crops and climate resilience.
The comparison between these pathways highlights an important insight. Bangladesh's greatest long-term challenge may not be producing enough food, but producing the right balance of foods to support healthier diets, reduce dependence on imports, and strengthen resilience to future shocks. This distinction has profound implications for agricultural policy over the coming decades.
Two futures, one choice
The comparison between the BAU and BAdj scenarios is not a competition between two agricultural models; rather, it represents two different policy choices. Under the BAU scenario, agricultural research continues, farmers adopt improved technologies, and crop productivity increases broadly in line with historical trends.
The BAdj scenario, by contrast, assumes that Bangladesh deliberately rebalances agricultural investments while protecting its greatest achievement -- rice security. In addition to sustained support for rice, greater attention is directed toward pulses, edible oil crops, maize, potatoes, and other nutritionally important crops that improve dietary quality and reduce import dependence.
The results demonstrate that rice remains the backbone of Bangladesh's food system under both scenarios. Population growth alone is projected to increase annual rice demand from about 38 million tons in 2024 to more than 48 million tons by 2074, making continued improvements in rice productivity indispensable.
Food diversification therefore does not imply reducing the importance of rice. Instead, it recognizes that while rice will continue to underpin national food security, other crops must play a larger role in addressing nutritional deficiencies that rice alone cannot meet.
The differences between the two scenarios become much more evident for non-rice crops. Pulses provide an excellent example. As one of Bangladesh's most affordable sources of plant protein, dietary fibre, iron, zinc, and other essential nutrients, pulses play a vital role in improving nutrition.
Yet domestic production has long failed to meet national demand. Under the BAdj scenario, strategic investments in improved varieties, quality seed systems, and better production technologies substantially increase pulse availability, strengthening national nutrition without compromising rice production.
A similar opportunity exists for edible oils. Bangladesh remains heavily dependent on imported edible oils, exposing consumers to international price volatility and supply disruptions. Expanding domestic production of mustard, soybean, sunflower, sesame, and other oilseed crops, while also increasing the extraction and utilization of rice bran oil from the country's abundant rice milling by-products, would strengthen nutritional security, reduce import dependence, add value to the rice sector, and enhance economic resilience.
Maize provides another important example. Although classified as a cereal, its principal contribution lies in supporting the poultry, livestock, and aquaculture industries. Increased maize production therefore strengthens the supply of eggs, milk, meat, and fish, thereby contributing indirectly to improved dietary quality and protein availability.
Potatoes also deserve greater policy attention. Bangladesh has already achieved remarkable gains in potato production, but further investments in storage, processing, value addition, and market development could transform potatoes from a seasonal surplus crop into a more stable contributor to food security, farm income, and rural employment.
Minor cereals, including millets, currently occupy only a small share of Bangladesh's agricultural landscape. However, as climate change intensifies, these hardy crops may become increasingly valuable in drought-prone and marginal environments, particularly in char lands and other stress-prone ecosystems. Rather than replacing rice, they can complement existing cropping systems by enhancing resilience in specific agroecological zones.
Collectively, these findings suggest that Bangladesh's future food challenge extends beyond increasing production. The central objective is to build a food system that delivers a balanced supply of nutritious foods while sustaining the country's hard-earned rice security.
Success should therefore be measured not only by total agricultural output but also by the extent to which the food system provides affordable, accessible, and nutritionally adequate diets for a growing population.
The balanced adjustment scenario is thus more than an alternative production pathway. It represents a long-term policy vision that preserves Bangladesh's remarkable achievement in rice security while progressively building a food system that is more nutritious, more diversified, more resilient, and better prepared for the challenges of the coming decades.
Ultimately, Bangladesh's choice is not between rice and diversification. It is between maintaining a food system designed primarily to eliminate hunger and developing one capable of eliminating both hunger and malnutrition.
Building the next agricultural transformation
Bangladesh's future food system will be shaped not only by changing dietary needs but also by powerful external forces. Climate change, shrinking agricultural land, water scarcity, labour shortages, environmental degradation, and increasing volatility in global food markets are already reshaping agricultural production. These pressures are expected to intensify over the coming decades, making agricultural transformation both an economic necessity and a national imperative.
Meeting these challenges will require more than producing larger quantities of food using yesterday's technologies. Future agricultural growth must be driven by innovation. Climate-resilient crop varieties, high-quality seed systems, precision agriculture, mechanization, artificial intelligence, satellite-based crop monitoring, digital advisory services, efficient water management, and reductions in post-harvest losses will all play increasingly important roles. Continued investment in agricultural research, innovation, and extension will therefore remain one of Bangladesh's most valuable long-term investments.
Equally important is food safety. Food security and nutrition security have limited value if the food itself is unsafe. Consumers increasingly expect food that is free from harmful contaminants, responsibly produced, and traceable throughout the supply chain.
Achieving this requires improvements not only in production but also in storage, transportation, processing, packaging, distribution, and marketing. Food safety should therefore be recognized not as a separate policy issue but as an integral component of agricultural development.
These realities call for a broader understanding of agricultural success. For decades, Bangladesh rightly measured progress primarily through increases in rice production because eliminating hunger was the nation's foremost priority. Today, however, success must also be evaluated in terms of dietary quality, nutritional outcomes, food safety, environmental sustainability, resource-use efficiency, and resilience to climate change.
Rice will remain the foundation of Bangladesh's food system because of its central role in national food security, farming systems, rural livelihoods, and cultural identity. Continued investment in advanced breeding, climate-resilient varieties, quality seed systems, efficient irrigation, mechanization, and improved crop management will therefore remain essential.
At the same time, greater attention should be directed toward expanding the production and value chains of pulses, oilseeds, rice bran oil, maize, potatoes, fruits, vegetables, fish, milk, eggs, and other nutrient-rich foods. The objective is not to replace rice, but to complement it with a more diverse and nutritious food basket.
This vision may be described as a rice-centred, nutrition-balanced food system. In such a system, rice continues to provide the foundation of national food security, while a diversified food basket supplies the proteins, healthy fats, vitamins, minerals, and dietary fibre required for healthy lives. Rather than competing with rice, these foods reinforce its role by creating a more resilient, nutritionally balanced, and sustainable food system.
Achieving this vision will also require stronger coordination across sectors. Agriculture alone cannot deliver nutrition security. Ministries responsible for agriculture, food, health, education, water resources, environment, trade, and local government must operate within an integrated policy framework.
Agricultural research, nutrition planning, food safety regulation, market development, consumer education, and social protection should reinforce one another rather than function as isolated initiatives. Such policy integration will become increasingly important as Bangladesh advances toward upper-middle-income status and confronts more complex development challenges.
Bangladesh has already demonstrated its ability to overcome seemingly impossible challenges. Few would have imagined fifty years ago that a country once synonymous with food shortages would become one of the world's leading rice producers. That extraordinary transformation illustrates the power of sustained investment in science, innovation, sound public policy, and the resilience of its farmers.
The next agricultural transformation now lies before the nation.
The first transformation Bangladesh must go through should be from chronic food deficit to rice security. The second must build upon that achievement to deliver nutrition security, safe food, environmental sustainability, and climate resilience. Rice should remain the country's strongest pillar of food security, but its success must now support a broader vision of healthy diets and sustainable development.
Bangladesh's future therefore does not lie in replacing rice. It lies in building upon the remarkable success of rice security to create a healthier, safer, more resilient, and more sustainable food system. If the first agricultural transformation enabled Bangladesh to win the battle against hunger, the next should enable it to win the battle against malnutrition while ensuring that every citizen has access to safe, nutritious, and sustainable food. That is the pathway toward a stronger Bangladesh over the next 50 years.
Dr Md Shahjahan Kabir is Former Director General, BRRI. He can be reached at Kabir.stat@gmail.com.

item.title: The art of the low blow. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There is a long-standing belief that politics is merely show business for ugly people.
In Bangladesh, however, it often feels less like theater and more like a rowdy neighbourhood brawl where the script was lost decades ago, replaced entirely by improvised insults.
Somewhere between the parliamentary floor and the election podium, the subtle craft of political satire died a quiet death.
In its place, our public figures have elevated character assassination, personal slurs, and visceral taunts into a primary form of governance.
What was once supposed to be parliamentary wit has devolved into a race to the gutter.
But as the decibel level of political mudslinging reaches a crescendo, an unsettling question emerges: Why is it that when politicians sling insults, it is called "strategy," but when ordinary citizens draw a caricature, it is treated as a crime against the state?
Political ribbing in Bangladesh was not always so coarse. In the immediate post-independence era, parliament and news archives recorded sharp, often humorous exchanges between legendary stalwarts.
Figures like Tajuddin Ahmad or Mawlana Bhashani were known to drop razor-sharp, sardonic observations that targeted policy and ideology rather than lineage or physical appearance.
Archival media reports from the 1970s and 1980s capture a period where politicians could trade barbed banter during the morning session and still share a cup of cha in the lounge by afternoon.
The decent masks fell off entirely during the nineties with the dawn of the " battling begums " era.
As Sheikh Hasina and Khaleda Zia traded turns at the helm, political rhetoric abandoned all subtlety.
The banter was no longer about fiscal policy or foreign affairs; it became deeply personal, bitter, and relentlessly petty.
Public rallies were reduced to arenas for scoring body blows -- mocking accents, personal wardrobe choices, family tragedies, and physical health.
Senior leaders quickly took cues from the top, realizing that a cheap, vulgar jab at an opponent yielded a louder roar from the rally crowd than a fifty-page manifesto ever could.
This toxic legacy set the standard for the generations that followed. Subtlety was out; public humiliation was in.
When verbal darts require an air ambulance
If anyone doubted that verbal vitriol could manifest as physical trauma, the recent pre-election spectacle between National Citizen Party (NCP) chief coordinator Nasiruddin Patwary and veteran BNP leader Mirza Abbas put those doubts to rest.
What began as standard electoral sparring in the high-stakes Dhaka-8 constituency rapidly degenerated into a public slugfest of toxic barbs, character assassination, and viral online taunts.
Patwary launched relentless, personal verbal missiles aimed at the senior leader, while egg-throwing incidents, street clashes, and retaliatory defamation lawsuits flooded the headlines.
The relentless barrage of insults, combined with the pressure of the campaign, took an unprecedented physical and psychological toll. In a turn of events that felt like a tragicomic climax to a dark political satire, the veteran BNP leader suffered a severe medical collapse mid-campaign.
Following brain surgery in Dhaka, Mirza Abbas had to be rushed via air ambulance to Singapore for emergency care.
When political banter reaches a point where it literally sends an opponent into a neuro-ICU halfway across the continent, it ceases to be "colour" or "flavour". It becomes a health hazard.
The audience's dilemma
Philosophically, the phenomenon raises a mirror to Bangladeshi society. Why do our politicians consistently take things too far?
The short answer lies in the dynamic between the performer and the crowd.
In a classic Roman sense, our political rallies function like the Colosseum.
The audience pretends to long for dignified statesmen who discuss inflation, institutional reform, and educational infrastructure.
Yet, the moment a politician steps up to the microphone and delivers a well-timed, vicious slur against their rival, the crowd erupts in cheers.
Clips of these low blows are clipped into 15-second TikTok videos, amplified with dramatic background music, and shared millions of times across Facebook.
We suffer from a national case of political schadenfreude. We claim to despise the lack of decorum, yet we reward the most toxic speakers with the highest engagement.
Politicians, who are fundamentally creatures of incentive, simply give the public what gets the loudest applause.
When policy bores the audience and insults electrify them, the politician will always choose the insult.
A subcontinental disease with global symptoms
Bangladesh is hardly alone in this descent into political vulgarity. Across our borders, regional neighbours demonstrate the exact same malaise:
The consequence in every single one of these nations is identical: The total erosion of public trust in state institutions, deep societal polarization, and a political environment so hostile that reasonable, capable minds refuse to enter public service.
The great double standard
The most sinister aspect of Bangladesh's political insult culture is not its coarseness, but its hypocrisy.
While politicians operate with complete impunity - slinging slander from stages and TV talk shows - ordinary citizens and artists who attempt true satire face the full, crushing weight of the state machine.
During the reign of the Awami League government, the state demonstrated a terrifying zero-tolerance policy toward actual humor.
Under the draconian Digital Security Act (DSA), cartoonist Ahmed Kabir Kishore was jailed and tortured simply for drawing caricatures that mocked the ruling elite’s handling of the pandemic.
Dissident writer Mushtaq Ahmed was thrown into high-security confinement for his critical social media posts, ultimately dying behind bars under suspicious circumstances.
This reveals a deeply broken dynamic: The state mechanism cannot stomach constructive satire, artistic parody, or citizen feedback.
Yet, the politicians running the state feel entitled to unleash unrestricted, crude verbal assault on each other.
When a society outlaws witty satire from its poets and cartoonists, humour does not disappear; it curdles. It mutates from artistic expression into the raw, unrefined malice of political mudslinging.
Restoring the punchline
Politics will always have room for sharp wit.
Some of the greatest political moments in world history involved brilliant, razor-sharp banter that exposed a rival’s hypocrisy without ever resorting to vulgarity.
When a society allows its politicians to replace substance with slurs, it forfeits its right to good governance.
Bangladeshi politics does not need fewer jokes; it needs better ones.
More importantly, it needs leaders who understand the difference between a witty parliamentary jab and a toxic verbal assault.
Until we as an audience stop rewarding the bullies at the podium, our political stage will remain a circus - and the joke, unfortunately, will continue to be on us.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.
